s: 70-metre Baroque hall, largest monastic library on Earth
w: Bartolomeo Altomonte's frescoes crown seven domes tracing knowledge toward divine wisdom, over a Late Baroque hall stretching 70 metres, the largest monastic library hall on Earth. Josef Stammler's grotesque wooden Four Last Things carvings lurk among shelves holding some 70,000 volumes.
why: The largest monastic library hall in the world, an unbroken 70-metre run of frescoed Baroque shelving inside a working Benedictine abbey.

s: Rococo hall of gilded shelves, 1,200 years of texts
w: Peter Thumb's Rococo hall, finished in 1767, holds 160,000 volumes on gilded wooden shelves beneath stucco cherubs and a fresco charting the path from folly to Christian truth. Visitors wear felt slippers to protect the parquet; the oldest treasure is an 8th-century illuminated Gospel book.
why: A UNESCO-listed Rococo library hall built around a monastic manuscript collection founded in the 8th century, among the oldest in continuous use.

s: Golden Baroque library on a cliff over the Danube
w: Jakob Prandtauer's Benedictine abbey holds a library of seven rooms, its main hall lined floor to ceiling in gilt-edged bindings beneath Paul Troger's ceiling fresco of Faith illuminating the world. Some 100,000 volumes, 1,800 manuscripts and 750 incunabula sit inside an abbey perched above the Danube.
why: One of Europe's grandest Baroque monastic libraries, its gilded shelving and painted ceilings crowning a cliff-top abbey overlooking the Danube.

s: Philip II's library, spines shelved facing inward
w: Juan de Herrera's barrel-vaulted hall for Philip II shelves books spine-inward, gilt page edges facing the room, a Renaissance quirk meant to protect the leather from dust. Frescoes by Pellegrino Tibaldi depict the seven liberal arts above 40,000 printed volumes and 4,700 manuscripts.
why: A royal Renaissance library where the books face backward on the shelves, built by Philip II to unite the humanities and sciences under one roof.

s: 17,000 Armenian manuscripts saved from every invasion
w: Named for the Armenian word for manuscript repository, this institute guards over 17,000 illuminated Gospels and royal decrees rescued across centuries of invasion, from a calendar weighing 19 grams to a homiliary weighing 28 kilograms. Mesrop Mashtots, inventor of the Armenian alphabet, stands in statue outside.
why: Armenia's national manuscript repository, holding one of the world's great collections of illuminated medieval texts saved through repeated conquest.

s: The Eye, terraced shelves ringing a glowing sphere
w: MVRDV's five-storey atrium terraces floor-to-ceiling shelving for 1.2 million books around a luminous spherical auditorium, earning it the nickname The Eye of Binhai. Many upper shelves are printed panels standing in for a collection still being filled, but the illusion draws over a million visitors yearly.
why: A dazzlingly photogenic modern library whose curved terraces of books wrap a glowing sphere, built in under three years for Tianjin's new cultural district.

s: Kalach's megalibrary, shelves floating over a whale
w: Alberto Kalach suspended steel bookshelves inside a vast atrium lit almost entirely by daylight, with Gabriel Orozco's whale skeleton, Ballena, hanging at its centre. Named for philosopher Jose Vasconcelos, it was built over a former railway yard to eventually hold two million volumes, ringed by desert gardens.
why: Mexico City's so-called megalibrary, a daylight-lit steel structure holding floating shelves around a suspended whale skeleton by Gabriel Orozco.

s: Nayak-era palm-leaf manuscripts inside a Maratha palace
w: Founded in the 16th century by Thanjavur's Nayak kings and expanded under the Maratha ruler Serfoji II, this palace library holds around 49,000 volumes, many of them palm-leaf manuscripts in Tamil and Sanskrit covering medicine, astronomy and music, among South Asia's most significant surviving collections.
why: One of Asia's oldest surviving libraries, its palm-leaf manuscript collection amassed by two dynasties inside a working royal palace.

s: A nawab's palace library of Mughal manuscripts and art
w: Built in 1904 inside the Rampur Fort palace complex, the Raza Library holds nearly 17,000 manuscripts in Arabic, Persian, Turkish and Urdu, alongside 5,000 Mughal and Rajput miniature paintings assembled by successive nawabs of Rampur, plus a jewelled astrolabe and Quranic pages annotated by Aurangzeb.
why: A princely-state library of rare Islamic manuscripts and Mughal miniatures, built inside a fort palace and still one of India's few protected monuments.

s: OMA's folded-plate library, one uninterrupted room
w: Rem Koolhaas's OMA folded a single concrete plate into terraced shelving that holds public, university and heritage collections inside one uninterrupted room, lit through a corrugated-glass facade. Sunk into a travertine-clad pit at its centre, the Heritage Library preserves rare Arab-Islamic manuscripts and maps.
why: A single vast folded-plate reading room by Rem Koolhaas's OMA, uniting Qatar's public, university and rare-manuscript collections under one roof.

s: A concrete cube with a glowing blue heart inside
w: Korean architect Eun Young Yi wrapped a stark grey concrete cube in nine-by-nine frosted glass bricks, then hid inside it a five-storey white hall he calls the Herz, or heart, spiralling upward around a single fountain and skylight. At night the whole building glows sapphire blue, floodlit from within.
why: A minimalist concrete cube that hides a luminous white spiral gallery inside, floodlit blue at night in Stuttgart's new Europaviertel district.

s: 27 glue-laminated timber ribs shaped like a whale
w: Helen and Hard's library is built from 27 prefabricated timber ribs, each bending to form structure, acoustic ducting, reading nook and bookshelf in one curved piece, together resembling a whale's ribcage. Built in 2011 from over 450 cubic metres of glulam wood, it earned Norway's top energy rating.
why: A small Norwegian library whose entire structure is built from 27 sculptural timber ribs that double as bookshelves, ducting and reading nooks.

s: Brutalist library raised on stilts over a book vault
w: Clorindo Testa's brutalist design, chosen by competition in 1961 but not finished until 1992, lifts its reading rooms on massive raw-concrete legs above underground stacks. The treasury holds a Gutenberg Bible leaf, while the fifth-floor room, where Jorge Luis Borges once served as director, looks over Recoleta.
why: Argentina's national library, a brutalist landmark on stilts where the blind writer Jorge Luis Borges once presided as director.

s: 22,000 desert manuscripts smuggled out ahead of militants
w: Abdel Kader Haidara founded this private library in 2000 to house his family's collection of some 22,000 manuscripts on law, astronomy, medicine and Quranic study, some dating to the 13th century. In 2012, as militants advanced on Timbuktu, staff smuggled the entire collection out by canoe and truck to Bamako.
why: A private Timbuktu manuscript library whose staff staged a daring rescue of 22,000 medieval texts ahead of an advancing militant occupation.

s: Secondhand books fill a Victorian railway station
w: Stuart and Mary Manley opened this shop inside Alnwick's disused 1887 railway station in 1991, spreading since through old waiting rooms and platforms across three miles of shelving. A model train runs above the stacks, and a framed Keep Calm and Carry On poster found here in 2000 sparked its modern revival.
why: One of Europe's largest secondhand bookshops, filling a preserved Victorian railway station and the birthplace of the Keep Calm poster revival.

s: Neo-Gothic bookshop with a blood-red spiral staircase
w: Francisco Xavier Esteves designed this 1906 shop for the Lello brothers, its stained-glass ceiling and carved wooden facade folding Neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau into one crowded room. A crimson staircase spirals through the centre, said to have caught the eye of J.K. Rowling while she taught English in Porto.
why: Widely called one of the world's most beautiful bookshops, its carved wood and crimson staircase said to have inspired J.K. Rowling.

s: Nine themed rooms, an Airstream and a parked Fiat
w: This bookshop splits its stock across nine wildly different rooms, a vintage Airstream trailer for travel titles, an Italian trattoria with a parked Fiat for cookbooks, and a blacked-out room where fiction hangs from the ceiling. Cafes and a cinema are folded into the maze, so a quick browse rarely stays quick.
why: A themed Brussels bookshop split into nine distinct rooms, from a trattoria with a parked car to a room of books hung from the ceiling.

s: A 13-metre bookshelf wall inside a shopping mall atrium
w: Two facing walls of shelving rise 13 metres through the atrium of COEX Mall in Gangnam, holding some 70,000 books and 600 magazines beneath a coffered glass roof. Built as a free public reading space rather than a shop, it draws crowds for its scale alone and glows under warm lamplight after dark.
why: A free public reading hall built inside a shopping mall, its 13-metre bookshelf walls making it one of Seoul's most photographed interiors.

s: Palm-leaf manuscripts inside the Temple of the Tooth
w: Established in 1875 within the grounds of Kandy's Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, this library preserves some 2,500 ola, or palm-leaf, manuscripts and 3,000 rare printed books on Sinhalese history, medicine and Buddhist doctrine, incised by hand into dried palm strips and bound with cord.
why: A palm-leaf manuscript archive kept inside Sri Lanka's most sacred Buddhist temple complex, preserving texts unique to the island.

s: Five tiers of cast-iron balconies rise to a skylight
w: Edmund Lind's 1878 stack room for philanthropist George Peabody rises 61 feet through five tiers of gold-scalloped cast-iron balconies to a latticed skylight, holding some 300,000 volumes mostly from the 18th and 19th centuries. Now part of Johns Hopkins, its symmetry makes it one of America's most photographed rooms.
why: A dramatic cast-iron stack room built for a 19th-century philanthropist's library, now among the most photographed interiors on the East Coast.

s: A Gothic reading room built for a university on a lake
w: The University of Washington's Graduate Reading Room stretches nearly the length of a football field beneath hammer-beam trusses and leaded windows depicting printers' marks from Gutenberg to Aldus Manutius. Named for a president who called the library the soul of the university, it still enforces hushed silence.
why: A collegiate-Gothic reading room modelled on a European cathedral, still enforcing hushed silence for students a century after it opened.

s: A Neo-Baroque palace's smoking room turned reading room
w: Housed inside the Wenckheim Palace, this branch of Budapest's public library system keeps its aristocratic interiors intact, dark panelling and gilt ceilings surrounding a spiral staircase in what was the palace smoking room, now quiet study space. Named for the sociologist who founded Hungary's library network.
why: A public library housed inside a former aristocratic palace, its gilt ceilings and smoking-room staircase preserved for everyday readers.

n: State Library of New South Wales
s: A 1913 domed reading room founded on convict-era books
w: Opened in 1856 with fewer than 4,000 books, the library's reading room added its copper-domed skylight in 1913, later restored after decades of leak-proofing had blocked the light. The Mitchell wing holds the world's largest collection on Australian exploration, from Captain Cook's own journals to convict records.
why: Australia's oldest library, its 1913 domed reading room sitting above the world's largest archive of Australian exploration and colonial history.

s: A hilltop Breton village of fifteen bookshops
w: Crowned a Book Town in 1989 following Hay-on-Wye's example, this fortified hilltop village near Rennes packs around fifteen bookshops, print studios and calligraphy workshops into streets built for a medieval market town. A monthly book fair fills the square, and the old ramparts look out over the Breton countryside.
why: A fortified medieval Breton village reinvented as a book town, its fifteen bookshops tucked into streets built centuries before the trade arrived.

s: A 500-year data vault buried in a frozen coal mine
w: Deep inside the disused Gruve 3 coal mine on Spitsbergen, this steel vault stores photosensitive film of digitised manuscripts and code from dozens of nations, chosen for permafrost cold and geological stability over internet uptime. The Vatican's archives and GitHub's open-source code both sit sealed inside.
why: A doomsday archive buried in an Arctic coal mine near the Global Seed Vault, storing the world's cultural memory on film built to last a millennium.

s: A financier's private palazzo of illuminated manuscripts
w: Charles McKim built this Italian Renaissance-style palazzo between 1902 and 1906 to house J. Pierpont Morgan's collection of illuminated manuscripts, old master drawings and rare printed books. Three gilded rooms and a tiered rotunda study opened to the public in 1924, once his son honoured his father's will.
why: A robber baron's private manuscript library turned public institution, its gilded rotunda study among Manhattan's most opulent interiors.

s: A cedar amphitheatre library open 24 hours, year-round
w: Mitsuru Senda's semicircular reading room at Akita International University is built almost entirely from local Akita cedar, its tiered wooden benches descending like a small amphitheatre beneath an umbrella roof. Known as the library that never sleeps, it stays open around the clock on a campus ringed by rice paddies.
why: Japan's only 24-hour, year-round library, a cedar amphitheatre built almost entirely from timber grown in its own home prefecture.

s: Three black rock-shaped libraries above a violent hillside
w: Giancarlo Mazzanti designed three faceted black volumes resembling boulders, perched above the Santo Domingo Savio barrio, once among Medellin's most violent. Built as part of the city's social urbanism program and reached by cable car, the library became a symbol of civic investment reclaiming poor hillsides.
why: A trio of boulder-shaped black library buildings built above a former conflict zone, emblematic of Medellin's transformation through public architecture.
